q: Ace Corp. had $100,000 of income from operations and received $20,000 of dividends from a domestic corporation in which it owns 10% of the stock. What is Ace's dividends-received deduction?
exp: A corporation owning less than 20% of the payer may deduct 50% of the dividends: 50% × $20,000 = $10,000. The taxable income limit (50% × $120,000 = $60,000) does not bind; $13,000 wrongly applies the 65% rate.

q: Bay Corp. owns 30% of a domestic corporation and received $100,000 of dividends from it. Bay also had a $10,000 loss from operations, so its taxable income before the dividends-received deduction is $90,000. What is Bay's dividends-received deduction?
exp: The full 65% DRD of $65,000 would not create a net operating loss ($90,000 − $65,000 = $25,000), so the deduction is limited to 65% of taxable income: 65% × $90,000 = $58,500. Taking the full $65,000 ignores the taxable income limitation.

q: Cove Corp. received $200,000 of dividends from a domestic company in which it holds a 10% stake and incurred a $110,000 operating loss, leaving $90,000 of taxable income before any DRD. What dividends-received deduction may Cove claim?
exp: The full 50% × $200,000 = $100,000 DRD would create a net operating loss ($90,000 − $100,000 = −$10,000), so the taxable income limitation does not apply and the full $100,000 is allowed. Limiting it to 50% × $90,000 = $45,000 overlooks the NOL exception.

q: Dell Corp. owns 85% of the stock of Elm Corp., and both are members of the same affiliated group. Elm paid Dell a $200,000 dividend. What percentage of the dividend may Dell deduct as a dividends-received deduction?
exp: Dividends from a member of the same affiliated group (generally 80% or more ownership) qualify for a 100% dividends-received deduction. The 65% rate applies to ownership of at least 20% but less than 80%.

q: Fox Corp. bought stock of a domestic corporation five days before the ex-dividend date and sold it ten days after the ex-dividend date. What is the effect on Fox's dividends-received deduction for the dividend received?
choices: No DRD is allowed because the stock was not held for more than 45 days during the required 91-day period
The DRD is allowed in full because Fox owned the stock on the record date
The DRD is reduced by half
The DRD is allowed but treated as a tax preference
exp: A corporation must hold the stock more than 45 days during the 91-day period beginning 45 days before the ex-dividend date to claim the DRD (§246). Owning the shares on the record date alone is not enough.

q: Gale Corp. made $120,000 of cash contributions to qualified charities this year. Its taxable income computed without the charitable contribution deduction, the dividends-received deduction, and any NOL or capital loss carrybacks is $800,000, which includes $100,000 of dividends eligible for a $50,000 DRD. What is Gale's charitable contribution deduction for the year?
exp: A corporation's charitable deduction is capped at 10% of taxable income computed before the charitable deduction and the DRD: 10% × $800,000 = $80,000. Computing the limit after subtracting the $50,000 DRD gives $75,000, which is the common error. For tax years beginning after 2025, contributions count only to the extent they exceed 1% of that same income ($8,000 here), which leaves $112,000 and does not change the $80,000 cap.

q: Corporate charitable contributions that exceed the annual percentage limitation are:
choices: Lost permanently
Carried back two years and forward 20 years
Carried forward for five years
Carried forward indefinitely
exp: Excess corporate charitable contributions are carried forward five years and are deductible in those years subject to the annual limitation, after current-year contributions. Indefinite carryforward applies to corporate NOLs, not contributions.

q: Hart Corp. had $200,000 of income from operations, a $10,000 long-term capital gain, and a $25,000 short-term capital loss this year. What is Hart's taxable income?
exp: A corporation may deduct capital losses only to the extent of capital gains, so the $15,000 net capital loss is not deductible this year and taxable income is $200,000; the excess is carried back three years and forward five. The $3,000 ordinary-income offset ($197,000) is available only to individuals.

q: When a corporation carries a net capital loss back or forward to another tax year, the loss is treated as:
choices: A short-term capital loss
A long-term capital loss
An ordinary loss
A loss of the same character it had in the year it arose
exp: Corporate net capital loss carrybacks and carryovers are treated as short-term capital losses in the year to which they are carried, and they offset only capital gains. Individuals, by contrast, keep the original character of their carryovers.

q: Iris Corp. had current earnings and profits of $40,000 and no accumulated E&P. It distributed $60,000 cash to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis was $15,000. How much capital gain does the shareholder recognize?
exp: $40,000 is a dividend from current E&P, $15,000 is a nontaxable return of capital that reduces basis to zero, and the remaining $5,000 is capital gain. Treating the entire $20,000 non-dividend portion as gain ignores recovery of basis.

q: Jade Corp. had current E&P of $30,000 and an accumulated E&P deficit of $50,000 at the beginning of the year. It distributed $40,000 cash to its sole shareholder during the year. What amount is a taxable dividend?
exp: Distributions are dividends to the extent of current E&P regardless of an accumulated deficit, so $30,000 is a dividend; the current and accumulated amounts are not netted when current E&P is positive. Netting them to a negative balance and concluding $0 is the classic mistake.

q: Kent Corp. began the year with accumulated E&P of $20,000 and had a current E&P deficit of $24,000 for the year, which accrued ratably. On June 30 (exactly half of the year), it distributed $15,000 to its sole shareholder. What amount is a taxable dividend?
exp: When current E&P is negative, the deficit is prorated to the distribution date and netted against accumulated E&P: $20,000 − ($24,000 × 1/2) = $8,000 dividend, with the rest a return of capital. Netting the full-year deficit gives $0, which is wrong for a midyear distribution.

q: Lark Corp. distributed land with an adjusted basis of $20,000 and a fair market value of $50,000 to its sole shareholder. Lark has ample E&P. What gain does Lark recognize, and what is the shareholder's dividend?
choices: $30,000 gain; $50,000 dividend
No gain; $20,000 dividend
No gain; $50,000 dividend
$30,000 gain; $20,000 dividend
exp: A corporation recognizes gain on distributing appreciated property as if sold at fair market value (§311): $50,000 − $20,000 = $30,000. The shareholder's dividend is measured by the property's $50,000 fair market value, not the corporation's basis.

q: Moss Corp., which has ample E&P, distributed land with a basis of $30,000 and a fair market value of $80,000 to its sole shareholder. The land was subject to a $20,000 mortgage that the shareholder assumed. What is the shareholder's basis in the land?
exp: A shareholder's basis in distributed property is its fair market value, $80,000; the liability reduces the amount of the distribution ($80,000 − $20,000 = $60,000 dividend) but not the basis. Using the $60,000 dividend amount as basis is the tempting error.

q: Nile Corp. distributed equipment with an adjusted basis of $50,000 and a fair market value of $35,000 to a shareholder as a nonliquidating distribution. What loss may Nile recognize?
choices: $15,000 ordinary loss
$15,000 capital loss
$15,000, deferred until the shareholder sells the equipment
exp: Under §311 a corporation recognizes gain, but not loss, on a nonliquidating distribution of property. Nile would need to sell the equipment and distribute the cash to recognize the $15,000 loss.

q: In computing current earnings and profits, which item is added to taxable income?
choices: Federal income taxes paid
Net capital loss in excess of capital gains
The nondeductible portion of business meals
Tax-exempt municipal bond interest
exp: Tax-exempt interest is economic income that increases E&P even though it is excluded from taxable income. Federal income taxes, excess capital losses and nondeductible meals are subtracted because they reduce the corporation's ability to pay dividends.

q: Opal Corp. had taxable income of $300,000, federal income tax of $63,000, tax-exempt interest of $10,000, and a dividends-received deduction of $15,000. Ignoring other adjustments, what is Opal's current earnings and profits?
exp: E&P = $300,000 + $10,000 tax-exempt interest + $15,000 DRD add-back − $63,000 federal tax = $262,000. Omitting the DRD add-back gives $247,000; the DRD is an artificial deduction that does not reduce E&P.

q: Pine Corp. reported book net income of $400,000. Its records show federal income tax expense of $84,000, tax-exempt interest income of $6,000, and a $10,000 net capital loss deducted for book purposes. What is Pine's taxable income?
exp: Taxable income = $400,000 + $84,000 federal tax expense + $10,000 nondeductible net capital loss − $6,000 tax-exempt interest = $488,000. Forgetting to add back the capital loss gives $478,000; corporations cannot deduct net capital losses.

q: On Schedule M-1, which item is added to book income to reconcile to taxable income?
choices: Proceeds of a key-person life insurance policy collected by the corporation
Tax-exempt municipal bond interest
Premiums paid on key-person life insurance when the corporation is the beneficiary
Tax depreciation in excess of book depreciation
exp: Premiums on life insurance where the corporation is the beneficiary are expensed for books but nondeductible, so they are added back. Policy proceeds and tax-exempt interest are subtracted because they are book income that is not taxable, and excess tax depreciation is also a subtraction.

q: Which corporations are required to file Schedule M-3 instead of Schedule M-1 with Form 1120?
choices: All publicly traded corporations, regardless of size
Corporations with gross receipts of $1 million or more
Corporations that have book-tax differences exceeding 10% of book income
Corporations with total assets of $10 million or more at the end of the year
exp: Schedule M-3 is required for corporations reporting total assets of $10 million or more on Schedule L at year-end; smaller corporations use Schedule M-1. The requirement turns on total assets, not gross receipts or public trading.

q: Quay Corp. distributed a pro rata common stock dividend on its common stock; shareholders had no option to receive cash or other property. How is the distribution treated by the shareholders?
choices: It is nontaxable, and shareholders allocate their existing basis between old and new shares
It is a taxable dividend equal to the fair market value of the new shares
It is taxable to the extent of the corporation's E&P
It is a taxable capital gain equal to the par value of the new shares
exp: Under §305 a pro rata stock dividend of common on common is generally excluded from income, and the shareholder's basis is allocated across old and new shares by relative value. It becomes taxable if any shareholder could elect cash or property instead.

q: On audit, the IRS determines that $150,000 of the salary Reed Corp. paid to its controlling shareholder-employee was unreasonable compensation. Reed has ample E&P. What is the effect?
choices: Reed may still deduct the $150,000, and the shareholder reports it as wages
Reed loses the deduction for the $150,000, and the shareholder reports it as a dividend
Reed loses the deduction, and the shareholder excludes the $150,000 from income
The $150,000 is treated as a loan from Reed to the shareholder
exp: Excess compensation to a shareholder-employee is recharacterized as a constructive dividend: nondeductible to the corporation and dividend income to the shareholder. The shareholder still has income; only its character changes.

q: Sage, an individual, owned 100 shares of Tull Corp. with a basis of $30,000. Tull redeemed all of Sage's shares for $100,000, and no family attribution rules apply because no relatives own stock. Tull has ample E&P. How does Sage treat the redemption?
choices: $100,000 dividend
$70,000 dividend
$70,000 capital gain
$100,000 capital gain
exp: A complete termination of the shareholder's interest under §302 is treated as a sale or exchange, so Sage recovers basis and recognizes $100,000 − $30,000 = $70,000 of capital gain. Dividend treatment applies only if the redemption fails all of the §302 exchange tests.

q: Vale owned 60 of the 100 outstanding shares of Wynn Corp. (the only class), and the rest were owned by unrelated persons. Wynn redeemed 30 of Vale's shares. Does the redemption qualify as substantially disproportionate under §302?
choices: No, because Vale still owns stock after the redemption
No, because Vale's ownership fell by only half
Yes, because Vale's ownership fell below 50% of the shares outstanding before the redemption
Yes, because Vale now owns 30 ÷ 70 = 42.9%, which is less than 50% and less than 80% of her former 60%
exp: After the redemption Vale owns 30 of 70 shares, or 42.9%, which is below 50% and below 80% × 60% = 48%, so the redemption is substantially disproportionate and gets exchange treatment. The test uses shares outstanding after the redemption, not before.

q: Xeno Corp. has a $500,000 net operating loss carryforward that arose in 2023. Its 2026 taxable income before the NOL deduction is $400,000. What is Xeno's NOL deduction for 2026?
exp: NOLs arising after 2017 may offset only 80% of taxable income: 80% × $400,000 = $320,000, and the remaining $180,000 carries forward indefinitely. Deducting $400,000 applies the pre-2018 rule that allowed a full offset.

q: Yard Corp., an accrual-basis calendar-year corporation, accrued a $50,000 bonus on December 31, Year 1, to its president, a cash-basis taxpayer who owns 60% of Yard's stock. The bonus was paid on February 15, Year 2. When may Yard deduct the bonus?
choices: Year 1, because it was paid within two and one-half months after year-end
Year 2, when the president includes the payment in income
Year 1, because all events fixing the liability occurred in Year 1
Never, because it is a payment to a majority shareholder
exp: Under §267, an accrual-basis payer may not deduct an amount owed to a related cash-basis payee (an individual owning more than 50% of the stock) until the payee includes it in income, so the deduction is in Year 2. The 2½-month rule applies only to unrelated employees.

q: Zane Corp. had a $100,000 net long-term capital gain and $500,000 of ordinary taxable income. How is the capital gain taxed?
choices: At a maximum rate of 20%
At a maximum rate of 15%
At the regular 21% corporate rate
At 21% only to the extent of capital losses carried forward
exp: Corporations do not receive a preferential rate on net capital gains; all taxable income, including capital gains, is taxed at the flat 21% rate. The 15% and 20% rates apply to individuals.

q: During the year Able Corp. paid $10,000 for client entertainment (a sporting event), $8,000 for business meals with clients at which business was discussed, and a $5,000 fine to a state agency for a regulatory violation. How much of these costs may Able deduct?
exp: Entertainment expenses are nondeductible, fines paid to a government are nondeductible, and business meals are 50% deductible: 50% × $8,000 = $4,000. Applying 50% to both entertainment and meals gives $9,000, which reflects pre-2018 law.

q: Brant Corp. had accumulated E&P of $100,000 before it distributed land with a basis of $20,000 and a fair market value of $50,000 to its shareholder. Ignoring income taxes, what is Brant's E&P after the distribution?
exp: E&P increases by the $30,000 gain recognized and then decreases by the $50,000 fair market value of the appreciated property distributed: $100,000 + $30,000 − $50,000 = $80,000. Subtracting $50,000 without first adding the recognized gain gives $50,000.

q: Which statement about the accumulated earnings tax is correct?
choices: It is self-assessed on Form 1120 by every corporation with accumulated E&P
It is imposed on earnings accumulated beyond the reasonable needs of the business to avoid shareholder-level tax on dividends
It applies to S corporations that were formerly C corporations
It is imposed on a corporation's total accumulated E&P regardless of business needs
exp: The accumulated earnings tax is a penalty tax on accumulated taxable income retained beyond reasonable business needs for the purpose of avoiding shareholder income tax, and it is assessed by the IRS rather than self-reported. Corporations may retain earnings up to reasonable needs and the statutory credit without penalty.
